subject: Archaeology
subcategory: Lost Cities of the Ancient World
title: Ayutthaya: Thailand's Fallen Capital
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Ayutthaya: Thailand's Fallen Capital.

hook.text: A Thai city was once the largest in the world. It was bigger than London when the Burmese burned it to ash.

buildup.text: Ayutthaya was founded in 1351 on an island between three rivers, with canals, temples, and global trade networks.

discovery.text: Foreign merchants from Japan, China, Persia, and Portugal had their own quarters inside the city walls.

twist.text: In 1767, the Burmese invaded and destroyed everything. They melted golden Buddhas and beheaded stone statues.

climax.text: Today, rows of headless Buddhas sit in the ruins. One famous head is tangled in the roots of a banyan tree.

punchline.text: A tree swallowed a Buddha's head. Nature finished what an army started.

quiz.question: What happened to Ayutthaya in 1767?
options: A catastrophic flood submerged the island city
The Burmese invaded and destroyed the city completely
A civil war between rival princes led to abandonment

details.summary: Ayutthaya served as the capital of the Siamese kingdom from 1351 to 1767 CE, when Burmese armies sacked and burned it. At its peak it was one of the world's largest cities, with over a million residents, elaborate temples, and a cosmopolitan population of Thai, Chinese, Japanese, and European.
details.whyItMatters: Ayutthaya demonstrates how thoroughly a major Asian capital could be destroyed by warfare. The Burmese sack was so devastating that the Siamese capital was permanently relocated to Bangkok, and Ayutthaya never recovered.
takeaways: Capital of the Siamese kingdom from 1351 to 1767 CE
One of the world's largest cities with over a million residents
Sacked by Burma in 1767, leading to its permanent abandonment

faq.question: How cosmopolitan was Ayutthaya?
faq.answer: It hosted permanent communities of Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch, French, and Persian merchants. Each community had its own quarter. European visitors compared it favorably to Paris and London. Its wealth came from controlling trade between China, India, and Southeast Asia.

faq.question: What survived the Burmese destruction?
faq.answer: Stone temple foundations, stupas, and prang towers survived because they could not burn. The Burmese deliberately beheaded Buddha statues and melted gold from temple decorations. Today the ruins — including a famous Buddha head entwined in tree roots — are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
